tier_reason: bench/bench_headline.cpp (MaxMulSK v3 vs Apple Accelerate vs OpenBLAS) is public with raw CSVs under bench/results/2026-09-09/; the compiler (Homebrew Clang 22.1.8, docs/BENCHMARKS.md), the flags (CMakeLists.txt) and the CPU (Apple M4) are all stated. Tier A covers the published v3 claim only. The v5.1 headline cannot be reproduced until its code is published.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Homebrew LLVM/Clang 22.1.8 (docs/BENCHMARKS.md). The bench_headline target compiles bench/bench_headline.cpp with -O3 -Wall -Wextra -mcpu=apple-m4 (no -fopenmp), and the v3 SME kernel and gemm_tuning sources with -march=armv8.7-a+sme+sme2 (CMakeLists.txt). OpenBLAS is loaded by dlopen with openblas_set_num_threads(1) and OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1. Accelerate is limited with VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS=1; the 29 September session pinned it with BLASSetThreading. For the SME-capable OpenBLAS the author built the develop branch with DYNAMIC_ARCH=1 (OPENBLAS_DIRECT_LIMIT=1792 in the 29 September session).
corrections.caveats: The headline v5.1 numbers (29 September 2026) come from a kernel whose code is not in the repository, measured with what the README calls 'the project's separate benchmark harness'. The reproducible claims are the published v3 path (bench/bench_headline.cpp, raw CSV in bench/results/2026-09-09/) and v4c versus Accelerate (bench/results/2026-09-13/v4c3.csv). v5.1 loses to Accelerate at 256^3 (0.74x) and is within 5% of OpenBLAS at 256^3 and 512^3 (0.98x, 1.03x). It trails MpGEMM at 256^3 (0.82x), at 512^3 (0.94x) and on two DeepSeek-V3 M=64 shapes (0.94x). MpGEMM's code is public (github.com/mpgemm/MPGEMM, MIT), and MaxMulSK benchmarks its row_sgemm entry point through the bench_vs_mpgemm target. The README says v3 trails Accelerate 'by 5 to 17% elsewhere', but its own 9 September table shows 0.97x at 2048^3. Timings of small calls depend on what ran just before them. macOS offers no thread pinning, run-to-run variance reaches 12% on the worst shapes, and the author treats differences under about 5% as noise. Homebrew's OpenBLAS cannot reach its SME kernels and falls off above 1024^3, so the author built OpenBLAS develop. Results are single-threaded FP32 on Apple M4 only (SME/SME2 required). It is a single-maintainer student project in a brand-new repository with 0 stars.

notes: The README numbers match the record: v3 1.01-1.31x on squares and 1.36-2.23x on LLM shapes against OpenBLAS; v5.1 4096^3 1732/1246/1595 GFLOP/s and 128x32768x512 1280 vs 370. The record wrongly calls MpGEMM code-less: github.com/mpgemm/MPGEMM exists (MIT, 11 stars, IPDPS '26, arXiv 2512.21473). The wave8 entry paper:mpgemm-arm-sme (repo_url null, has_code false) should be updated with that repository.

corrections.caveats: The headline figure is from one 2021 run with a Julia 1.7 development build on an 18-core/36-thread i9-10980XE (Cascade Lake-X) using 36 threads. Only the 1000x1000x1000 row is printed as numbers; other sizes appear only in an SVG plot. MKL, OpenBLAS and BLIS versions are not stated, and newer versions of them, or of Julia and LoopVectorization, may change the ranking. The result is multi-threaded; single-thread results and other CPUs are not shown. Commits in the last year are CI and dependency bumps only (latest 2025-10-21). Octavian depends on LoopVectorization.jl, whose maintenance now relies on the SciML Small Grants program. It is pure Julia, not a C++-callable library. The README says the full size sweep took 2h25m.

notes: The README numbers match the record exactly: at 1000^3, median GFLOPS were 1816 for Octavian, 1254 for OpenBLAS, 1348 for MKL and 1051 for BLIS. The page confirms MIT, 255 stars and the last commit on 2025-10-21; that commit was a dependabot CI bump.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.13: Project.toml compat julia = "1.13" and LinearAlgebra = "1.13.0", and CI tests only 1.13. The exact patch release, LLVM and OpenBLAS_jll versions used for the sweep are not stated. Default JIT optimization (no custom flags). The harness is bench/plots.jl with BLAS.set_num_threads(1), BLIS_NUM_THREADS/OMP_NUM_THREADS pinned to 1 before AOCL loads, and PureBLAS called through its native API against LinearAlgebra.BLAS. Frequency is locked with bench/fleet_freqlock.sh (boost off, base clock) and runs use ABBA-interleaved rounds with the median ratio reported. Reproduce: taskset -c N julia --project=bench bench/plots.jl bench. AOCL comes from AOCL_jll (amd-main).
corrections.caveats: This is a very young project (9 stars). The benchmarks are the project's own and run only on three AMD Zen machines; the Zen5 box is a laptop whose worst cells move by several points between runs, and there are no Intel or Arm results in the table. The table shows a per-op median with the worst cell, so some cells lose: gemm worst 0.94 on Zen4 and 0.90 on Zen5, and docs/src/notes.md lists trmm on AVX2 at 0.84 as still open. That notes page also says gemm 'gates at every size on all three boxes', which conflicts with the table's worst cells. Above about min(m,n,k) >= 256, gemm uses Strassen-Winograd (notes.md, ROADMAP.md), so the gemm and BLAS-3 ratios compare a fast-matrix-multiplication algorithm with weaker error bounds against OpenBLAS's classical gemm. Some large ratios reflect weak reference implementations rather than kernel speed: nrm2 runs at 8-11x, and methodology.md itself warns about packed Cholesky and small-n AOCL. The README says about 87% of benchmarked cells are at or above max(OpenBLAS, AOCL). methodology.md gives per-cell drift of 1-6% and says about 30% of cells sit within +-5% of parity. notes.md compares potrf against BLASFEO as an MKL proxy (0.87-1.04x), not against MKL directly. All code is single-threaded. The C-callable shared library depends on experimental juliac --trim.

notes: Every gemm, potrf, getrf and geqrf figure in the record matches bench/gen_table.md. The page confirms MIT, 9 stars and the last commit on 2026-09-30. The main new shortcoming is that gemm uses Strassen-Winograd at large sizes, so it is not like-for-like with classical BLAS on numerics.
